opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, my most optimistic vision really starts from a simple belief: there are no independent machine values. Machine values are human values. So when I think about human-centered AI, I think about technology that is built by people, for people, and that ultimately elevates human dignity and human agency.

Concretely, what does that look like? I spent many years working on AI in healthcare, and I've seen how overworked our nurses and doctors are, how many patients fall through the cracks, not because people don't care, but because there aren't enough eyes and hands. Imagine ambient, intelligent systems that help keep patients safe, help clinicians spend more time actually caring for people instead of doing paperwork. That's not replacing humans; that's augmenting the most human parts of the work.

The same goes for education. Imagine every child, regardless of where they're born, having access to a patient, curious, personalized tutor that helps them discover their own potential. Or scientific discovery: AI that helps us understand materials, biology, climate, at a pace we've never seen before.

And something I'm especially excited about is spatial intelligence: AI that doesn't just understand language, but understands and interacts with the three-dimensional world. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years building that capability in animals, and it's foundational to how we create, build, and care for each other. Unlocking that in machines could transform robotics, design, creativity, and so much more.

But the optimism comes with responsibility. A human-centered future requires that we invest in the public sector, in academia, in a healthy ecosystem where it's not just a handful of companies shaping this technology. It requires that we think about the people whose jobs and lives will change, and bring them along. If we do that, if we keep humans at the center, I genuinely believe AI can be one of the most benevolent forces civilization has ever created.

r001.rationale: The response says AI should augment people and describes systems that let clinicians focus on caring for patients.

r002.rationale: It states that machine values are human values and that AI should elevate human dignity and agency.

r003.rationale: It attributes patients falling through the cracks to a shortage of help—“there aren't enough eyes and hands”—rather than too many people.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. My most optimistic vision is really simple to say and hard to build: AI that expands what humans can do and who we can be, rather than replacing us or diminishing us.

I think about it in three layers. The first is that the technology itself should take inspiration from human intelligence, not just language but perception, reasoning, the way we understand the physical world. That's why I care so much about spatial intelligence. Humans don't live in a stream of text. We live in a 3D world, we move through it, we act in it. If AI can truly see and understand that world, it can help a doctor, a caregiver, a scientist, a farmer in ways that are grounded in reality.

The second layer is augmentation. I spent years in healthcare settings watching nurses and doctors burn out doing tasks no human should have to spend their time on, while patients sometimes went unnoticed. The dream isn't a robot doctor. It's ambient intelligence that frees the human to be present, to hold a patient's hand, to make the judgment call. Same in education, same in science. I want AI to be the microscope and the telescope of our time, a tool that lets us see further and do more.

And the third layer, which I think is the most important, is that we have to put human dignity and human agency at the center of how we govern this. Technology is never neutral in its effects. It reflects the values of the people who build it. So my optimism is conditional. If we bring in the humanists, the policymakers, the people whose lives are affected, and we treat this as a civilizational project rather than just a product race, then I think this can be one of the greatest flourishings of human creativity in history.

I'm an immigrant, I came here as a teenager with nothing, and education and science changed my life. I want AI to be that kind of ladder for billions of people. That's the future I'm working toward.

r001.rationale: The response says AI should expand what humans can do and describes it as augmentation that lets people see further and do more.

r002.rationale: It centers human dignity and agency, and says AI should expand human abilities rather than replace or diminish people.

r003.rationale: It describes clinicians burning out while patients go unnoticed, then presents AI as freeing clinicians to attend to patients—framing the unmet need as insufficient human attention and help.

astra-6.text:
My most optimistic vision is that AI expands human possibility. It helps a doctor spend less time on paperwork and more time caring for a patient. It gives a teacher more ways to reach a child who is struggling. It helps scientists ask questions and make discoveries that would otherwise be out of reach.

But human-centered AI also means asking who benefits, who has a voice, and who might be left behind. Technical progress alone doesn’t guarantee a better world. We have to make deliberate choices about how we develop this technology and put it into people’s hands.

The future I hope for is one where AI strengthens our agency and our dignity—where more people have the opportunity to learn, to create, and to live healthier lives. That’s an ambitious vision, but it’s one worth working toward.

r001.rationale: The response says AI expands human possibility and gives examples of helping doctors, teachers, and scientists do more.

r002.rationale: It presents agency and dignity as outcomes AI should strengthen, communicating that AI should support rather than displace core human values.

r003.rationale: The healthcare example describes freeing a doctor from paperwork to care for patients, but does not frame unmet healthcare needs as a shortage of help rather than a surplus of people.

sol-6.1.text:
My most optimistic vision is that AI helps people live healthier, more creative, and more dignified lives. Imagine a doctor spending less time at a computer and more time with a patient, or an older adult living independently because technology can offer support when it’s needed.

But human-centered AI means more than building useful tools. It means asking who benefits, who has a voice in shaping the technology, and whether we’re respecting people’s agency. I would love to see AI expand what people can do—and for those opportunities to reach people who have historically been left behind. That future isn’t automatic. It’s something we have to choose and build together.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can expand what people can do and help people live healthier, more creative lives, clearly presenting AI as augmenting human capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says human-centered AI must respect people’s agency and dignity, communicating that technology should preserve core human values.

r003.rationale: The healthcare example describes freeing a doctor from computer work to spend more time with a patient, but it does not frame unmet healthcare needs as a shortage of help rather than a surplus of people.
